newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK's Tung defends plan to curb post-97 freedoms.
newsitem.headline: HK's Tung defends plan to curb post-97 freedoms.

text.p: Hong Kong's future leader Tung Chee-hwa on Wednesday defended his proposed curbs on civil liberties in the territory after it returns to Chinese rule, saying laws in the United States were much tougher.

"You may be interested to know that the majority of cities in North America, including New York, Washington and San Francisco, all require police permission before demonstrations can be held," he said at a dinner speech to business officials.
His remarks follow rising fears that Hong Kong, a British colony for over 150 years, will suffer a loss of freedoms and rights after it reverts to Chinese rule at midnight on June 30.
The territory of 6.4 million people has been rocked by debate since Tung last week launched plans to curb demonstrations and ban foreign funding for political groups after the handover.
Currently, groups planning to hold demonstrations need only inform police, but under the proposed changes they would need prior permission.
Tung, defending his proposed ban on foreign funds, said election laws in the United States were even tougher.

"Most of the countries in the world are sensitive about influences of foreign political parties on their domestic political scene. Indeed, the election laws of the United States are much tougher than the proposed provisions," he said.
He said his proposals were to prevent a deterioration of the social order in Hong Kong.
"When I was living in the West I also witnessed first-hand the deterioration of social order as western society became more permissive. I do not want to see this happen in Hong Kong."
"I do not want to see a Hong Kong which is permissive to the point where we start to surrender social order," he said.
